sections.title: Two businesses, one backlog
ps: A {{neocloud}} owns GPUs and rents time on them; a landlord owns a hall and rents it for years under a {{colocation}} lease while the tenant brings the servers. WhiteFiber is both: a GPU cloud (GB300, B300, H100 and VR200 systems on a 3.2 Tb/s fabric) and a data-centre arm that leases a Montreal hall to a chip company for five years and a North Carolina campus to Nscale for ten.

The two businesses earn differently. Cloud revenue is recognised as hours are used, and a customer that stops using them stops paying: the customer that was 70.7% of 2025 revenue was terminated in 2026. Rent is owed whether or not the tenant's GPUs are busy.

{{Remaining performance obligations}} are contracted revenue not yet earned. At mid-2026 the company carried about US$1,008 million of them: US$933 million from colocation and US$75 million from cloud. Most of today's revenue is cloud; 93% of tomorrow's is one lease.

sections.title: The retrofit: buying a feed, not a floor
ps: {{Adaptive reuse}}: the company converts factories rather than building shells. A yarn plant of about 1,000,000 square feet became NC-1; a mattress factory became MTL-3; two more textile buildings are NC-2 and NC-3. It says a retrofit takes about six months at US$8 to 10 million per gross megawatt, against an industry average it puts at US$13 million.

The value is the electrical history. A factory that ran spinning lines already has a utility service agreement, a {{substation}} and a transmission tap. NC-1 inherited the plant's {{electric service agreement}} by assignment, which is why 54 gross MW arrived within a year of purchase without a new large-load interconnection.

The price was written in megawatts: the seller earns US$8 million more if the utility delivers or contracts at least 99 MW within two years, US$5 million within three, and US$200,000 for every megawatt above 99. An {{earn-out}} on power, not on profit.

sections.title: A letter is not a service agreement
ps: **The letter.** The utility's 16 May 2025 {{letter agreement}} states an estimated peak load of 99 MW at 24 kV and promises 'commercially reasonable efforts' to deliver 24, 40 and 99 gross MW on a schedule, adding that it 'does not guarantee timelines can be met'. The final phase is due within four years, by May 2029.

**The agreement.** The executed {{electric service agreement}} is the one inherited from the yarn plant, with a minimum monthly bill of US$8,754. The company's annual report says no agreement for more than 99 MW has been received.

**The tariff.** Every term defers to tariffs approved by the state commission, which is writing a {{large-load tariff}} in a separate proceeding before 2027 rates take effect. Whatever minimum bill and term it sets will govern the next phases.

**The contrast.** At another landlord's Ohio site the transmission owner records that 'the customer will own' the substation. Same wire, opposite property line: there the customer buys the transformers and breakers too. Ask which model a site uses before asking who buys what.

sections.title: Medium-voltage switchgear: the item that delays a lease
ps: {{Medium voltage}} {{switchgear}} is a lineup of metal-enclosed cabinets at 5 to 35 kV holding circuit breakers, disconnects, protection relays and metering. It takes the utility's feed, protects the site against faults and splits the power into feeders for the transformers that step it down to the 480 V the UPS and racks use: the site's main fuse box at the scale of a building.

It is on the critical path because every downstream item is tested against a live medium-voltage bus. No switchgear, no bus, no {{commissioning}}. {{Lead time}}s for medium-voltage gear have run 12 to 18 months in the current cycle, and the relays and breakers inside come from a short list of makers.

The company's words, in order: 'a recently identified supply-chain-related issue affecting certain medium-voltage switchgear components' (May); 'not a broad equipment availability issue', with delivery as 'a scaled ramp-up' (the same call); 'delivering and commissioning issues involving certain switchgear equipment. Those issues have since been resolved' (August).

The cost: two 20 MW phases due 30 April and 30 May began billing in the third quarter, with the full run rate expected in August. Roughly a quarter of rent on a lease worth about US$7 million a month. The utility's substation was on time; the delay sat inside the customer's own scope. No supplier is named anywhere.

sections.title: Who signs the order, and for what
ps: **The customer of record.** Everything behind the utility's meter is bought by the landlord's site company: medium-voltage switchgear, transformers, UPS, generators, direct-to-chip cooling for two 20 MW phases, and the same list again at the 60 to 200 MW Yadkin County sites from 2027.

**The demonstrated gap.** The only place on this record where that buying authority was exercised and failed is medium-voltage switchgear. A vendor that can deliver it on a six-month retrofit schedule is selling into a documented pain.

**What is not bought.** The substation and transformers on the utility side; the fuel cells, which a third-party provider would own and operate; and any battery, {{SST}} or {{800 VDC}} project, none of which appears on the company's channels.

sections.title: What a cloud rating measures
ps: {{ClusterMAX}} tests a cloud's networking, orchestration, monitoring and security attestation by renting it and running jobs. This company's networking was 'within the reference numbers if not slightly better'; its Slurm and Kubernetes layer did not work; it had no SOC 2 or ISO 27001 attestation. Result: 'Not Recommended – Underperforming', kept in the next edition without a re-test.

The rating says nothing about the halls. A landlord's product is power, cooling and uptime under a lease; the cloud's product is a working scheduler on a fast fabric. That is why the same company can be worth more as a landlord than as the cloud the rating describes.

sections.title: Where new power technology would enter
ps: **Fuel cells.** The stated intent is natural-gas {{fuel cell}} generation {{behind-the-meter}} 'by partnering with third-party energy providers'. A fuel cell converts gas to electricity electrochemically, in modular blocks; the provider owns them and sells the power. The landlord signs a power contract, not an equipment order.
**Batteries.** The only mention is a supply-chain risk factor on battery systems that transit Mexico: {{UPS}} batteries, not a storage project.

**SST and 800 VDC.** Nowhere on the company's channels. A retrofit reuses a 24 kV feed and conventional transformers; racks are {{NVL72}}-class at up to 150 kW per cabinet on standard 480 V distribution. A {{solid-state transformer}} or an {{800 VDC}} bus would first make sense at the 2027 sites, designed from scratch, if a tenant asked.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **One lease.** 93% of the backlog is one tenant, itself dependent on one hyperscaler; the tenant's loan for the site matures 'on the date on which the customer makes its final scheduled payment'.
**A cloud that misses.** Three of the first four quarterly results missed consensus by wide margins; the largest customer was terminated; the independent rating is below Bronze.
**A parent that lends.** Control at 59.9% and falling with each issue; a related-party loan at 9.5% funded by borrowing against a cryptocurrency at 5.45%.
**A county that pauses.** The next two sites sit inside a town whose county adopted a two-year {{moratorium}} the day after they were announced; the town says its limits exempt them.

cards.q: What are remaining performance obligations, and why can one lease dominate them?
cards.a: Contracted revenue not yet earned. A ten-year lease books a decade of rent at signing; cloud contracts are short and are earned as hours are used.

cards.q: What is the difference between gross MW and IT MW?
cards.a: Gross is what the utility delivers to the whole site; IT is what the servers draw. PUE links them: at 1.3, 40 MW of IT needs about 52 gross MW.

cards.q: Where does the utility's equipment end at a site with a utility-owned substation?
cards.a: At the meter, after the substation, transformers, breakers and metering it owns as 'Extra Facilities' and recovers through a monthly charge. The customer's scope starts at the medium-voltage switchgear.
Takes the utility's feed at 5 to 35 kV, protects the site with breakers and relays, and splits it into feeders for the transformers that step it down to the voltage the UPS and racks use.

cards.q: Why can late switchgear components delay a lease that the utility has already powered?
cards.a: Every downstream item is commissioned against a live medium-voltage bus; without the switchgear nothing downstream can be energised, so rent cannot start.

cards.q: What is the difference between a utility's letter agreement and an executed electric service agreement?
cards.a: A letter promises commercially reasonable efforts on a schedule and guarantees nothing; a service agreement commits to serve a stated load under the tariff.

cards.q: How can a parent's stake fall ten points without selling a share?
cards.a: The subsidiary issues new shares, for example in a convertible-note exchange; control dilutes by issuance.

cards.q: What is a related-party loan, and why does it need fairness opinions?
cards.a: A loan between companies that share control or management; independent committees and outside opinions are needed because the lender and borrower cannot bargain at arm's length.

cards.q: Who buys the fuel cells when a data centre 'partners with third-party energy providers'?
cards.a: The provider, which owns and operates them; the data centre signs a power contract, not an equipment order.

cards.q: What does a ClusterMAX rating test, and what does it not?
cards.a: The cloud: networking, orchestration, monitoring, security attestation. Not the halls: power, cooling, uptime under a lease.

items.q: A company reports US$29 million of quarterly revenue, four-fifths cloud, and a US$1.0 billion backlog, 93% colocation. Which business is the balance sheet built on?
c: The cloud, because it earns most revenue
The colocation, because the backlog is what can be financed
items.why: {{Remaining performance obligations}} are what lenders borrow against, and here they are almost entirely one lease.

items.q: A lease says 40 MW of IT and the utility's letter says 99 MW. At a PUE of 1.3, how much IT load could 99 gross MW carry?
The utility finished its substation in May and the tenant's rent started in August. Where did the three months go?
c: Inside the customer's scope: medium-voltage switchgear components late or failing commissioning
items.why: The company's own disclosures place the delay on 'certain medium-voltage switchgear components' and their commissioning; the utility side was on time.

items.q: Which document commits a utility to serve a stated load?
c: A letter agreement promising commercially reasonable efforts
An executed electric service agreement under the tariff
items.why: The letter guarantees nothing; the {{electric service agreement}} is the contract.

items.q: A parent pledges not to sell shares in 2026, yet its stake falls from about 70% to about 60%. Why?
c: The subsidiary issued about 6.3 million new shares in a note exchange
items.why: Dilution by issuance: the parent's share count was fixed while the total grew.

items.q: What is the first thing the customer owns after the meter at a site with a utility-owned substation?
c: The step-down transformers on the utility side
items.why: Under the assigned agreement the utility owns the lines, substation, transformers, breakers and metering as Extra Facilities; the customer's chain starts at its {{switchgear}}.

items.q: A data centre intends fuel-cell generation 'by partnering with third-party energy providers'. What does it sign?
c: A power contract with the provider that owns the cells
items.why: The provider owns and operates the {{fuel cell}}s; the data centre is the offtaker.
